rv.q: Wonderful Sutton Foster and thrilling, dirt-kicking musical.
Driven by a performance of incandescent yearning from Sutton Foster that’s all the more moving for its restraint, Violet is a delicate wildflower, craning toward the sun.
Ms. Foster moves into thornier territory than she has occupied before in frothy musicals like “Thoroughly Modern Millie,” “The Drowsy Chaperone” and the recent revival of “Anything Goes.”
At its best, Violet is a rare example of how song can work to bind all the elements of theater into moments so rich with information they are almost overwhelming.
Let’s hope so, because helmer Leigh Silverman and collaborating creatives have done a lovely job of reviving this winsome 1997 musical by Brian Crawley (book & lyrics) and Jeanine Tesori (music).

Sunday April 20 2014ShareCopy LinkFacebookTwitterPinterestEmailWhatsAppBuy ticketAdvertisingTime Out saysViolet. Theatre (see Broadway). Music by Jeanine Tesori. Book and lyrics by Brian Crawley. Directed by Leigh Silverman. With Sutton Foster, Joshua Henry, Colin Donnell. Running time: 1hr 45mins. No intermission.
In these all-important moments, the storytelling becomes muddied and you don't get the emotional payoff I've seen with this piece before.
And with Sutton Foster in the title role, its Broadway premiere is an absolute triumph that should not be missed.
And what a wonderful trip it is.
You’ll feel as though you’re witnessing a star being reborn, 18 years into her career.

It’s impossible not to get swept up by rousing numbers like Violet’s ”On My Way” and Flick’s ”Let It Sing” (Henry pretty much blows the roof off the bus with that one) — or to resist Foster’s pluck and aw-shucks charm.
Sutton Foster, a two-time Tony winner, gives her most expressive, deeply felt and vibrant performance to date, fully capturing the character's yearning and volatility.
As Violet – the woman with a dream to shoot out of her life and into a new world
Sutton Foster proves she can do anything with her brilliantly grounded yet soaring performance in Violet
Silverman and her cast reward our patience with performances that transcend clichés.

The moment Violet encounters the evangelist, who's with his choir, you know the singers will perform a rousing hallelujah number ("Raise Me Up"), led by an African-American woman (Rema Webb). The takeaway from the show, after Violet finds love but not physical transformation, is that true beauty lies within.
"Violet" is a reminder — if we have already forgotten the power of "Once" — that a Broadway musical has to hit your heart as much as be visually pretty.

cn.t: Critics embrace this intimate, emotionally resonant musical, praising Tesori's rich score and Foster's restrained, luminous performance. A few find the story too familiar or fragile, but most celebrate its modest scale and heartfelt beauty.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
